extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, IP litigators, biotech/pharma stakeholders, and IP scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and applying the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph, particularly as it affects claim scope (genus vs species) and biotechnology/chemical inventions. Focuses on how the specification must show 'possession' of the invention and the limits of relying on enablement or generic claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate written description requirement (distinct from enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112, first paragraph, contains two separate description requirements: a written description of the invention and a written description of how to make and use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held that adequacy of the written description is not determined solely by enablement; grammatical/parallelism arguments do not collapse the two requirements. The decision relies on precedent (e.g., Regents of University of California v. Eli Lilly) and cites stare decisis as a reason to preserve the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must demonstrate 'possession' of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification itself must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention; actual possession or reduction to practice outside the specification is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession language has been used historically although it may be 'not very enlightening'; nevertheless, the specification must show in a definite way that the inventor possessed the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice can satisfy written description; actual examples not strictly required
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement does not demand either examples or an actual reduction to practice; a constructive reduction to practice that in a definite way identifies the claimed invention can satisfy the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Falko-Gunter Falkner v. Inglis. However, the specification must still show possession — mere theoretical description without sufficient concrete disclosure may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description does not require reciting claim terms verbatim, but mere obviousness is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not recite the claimed invention 'in haec verba', but a description that merely renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Carnegie Mellon Univ. v. Hoffmann-La Roche and Lockwood v. American Airlines. Showing how to get to the invention by obvious steps is not the same as demonstrating possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line rule for number of species to support a genus claim; fact-specific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court will not set bright-line rules (e.g., a fixed number of species required to adequately describe a genus); satisfaction depends on the facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different facts lead to different outcomes; Wands factors and the state of the art (e.g., primitive/uncertain arts) will influence whether disclosure supports a genus claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional (result-oriented) genus claims require specification to recite sufficient materials to accomplish the claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent claims a genus by its function or result, the specification must recite sufficient materials to accomplish that function and demonstrate a generic invention that achieves the claimed result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly emphasized for biological arts: functional claim language that merely claims a desired result without describing species that achieve the result will fail written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claim language in the original specification does not automatically satisfy written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic claim language appearing in the original specification does not satisfy the written description requirement if it fails to support the scope of the genus claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court uses the 'black box' analogy: defining boundaries without describing contents is insufficient. Cases cited include Fiers, Eli Lilly, and Enzo v. Genprobe as examples where generic language failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description applies to original and amended claims alike
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no principled basis to distinguish original claims from amended claims for purposes of the written description requirement; even original claims can encompass subject matter not sufficiently described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement is not limited to policing priority; claims alone do not guarantee that the specification disclosed invention adequate to support claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define boundaries/notice but are not a substitute for specification disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims 'define the subject matter' and provide notice of the boundaries of the patentee's right to exclude, but their purpose is not to describe the invention — the specification must do that job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court emphasized that relying on claims to serve as the descriptive disclosure risks treating claim language as after-the-fact boundary-setting rather than description of what the inventor actually invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description serves to prevent overbroad claims that preempt future invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement helps curtail claims that do not require undue experimentation to make and use (and thus may satisfy enablement) but that have not been invented and thus cannot be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites policy concerns (e.g., Brenner v. Manson) that patents are compensation for a successful conclusion, not a reward for research; written description prevents preempting the future before it has arrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular importance of written description in chemical and biotechnological arts
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate written description requirement plays a vital role in curtailing claims in chemical and biotech fields where enablement may be satisfied without the inventor having actually invented species within a broad genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court stressed biotechnological examples where genus-by-function claims could claim a result without disclosing sufficient species; the doctrine is especially protective in unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction of written description is a question of fact influenced by the Wands factors and the state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Different factual records produce varied conclusions; factors used in enablement analysis (e.g., Wands) and the primitive/uncertain state of the art can bear on written description sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although related to enablement inquiries, written description analysis remains a separate factual question; courts will examine the record (e.g., priority dates, evidence presented at trial) to determine sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must provide sufficient species or a descriptive formula to identify others for broad genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To support broad genus claims, the specification normally should identify a number of species and/or provide a descriptive formula or guidance enabling a PHOSITA to identify other species that fall within the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is 'no magic number' of species — what suffices depends on the technology and predictability; academic disclosures that stop at mechanism without describing useful compounds often fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: avoiding recitation of species to skirt prior case law is disapproved
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies that attempt to avoid reciting specific molecules or species in claims to escape prior-case holdings (e.g., avoiding naming NF-kB inhibitors) are disfavored and may be rejected under written description analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court specifically disapproved Ariad's approach of omitting molecule examples to circumvent prior decisions (e.g., University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement remains a distinct doctrine focused on undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement (the requirement to teach how to make and use the invention without undue experimentation) remains separate from written description, which focuses on demonstration of invention/possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although overlap exists and both inquiries may consider similar evidence, courts will analyze enablement (often via Wands factors) separately from written description sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis and settled expectations weigh against overturning longstanding written description doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Federal Circuit has long applied a written description requirement, principles of stare decisis counsel caution in changing the doctrine — changes should rest with Congress rather than judicial reversal absent good reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court noted it must 'tread lightly' to avoid disrupting inventing/investing communities and PTO practice; this influences doctrinal continuity but not the substance of case-by-case analysis.
